list.listitem: Diagnosis is based on clinical recognition of typical skin, nail, and scalp lesions. C
Multiple types of psoriasis exist, making it essential to know the patterns for the less common types including inverse psoriasis and palmoplantar psoriasis. C
Topical corticosteroid monotherapy or combination therapy with topical vitamin D/corticosteroid is the first line treatment for mild psoriasis. A
Consider phototherapy for more extensive disease. B

Systemic therapies, including methotrexate and biologics, are useful for extensive or resistant disease, but require close monitoring due to the potentially serious side effects. Biologic agents (monoclonal antibodies) are increasingly becoming the standard of care, particularly when other agents such as methotrexate have failed. A

background.definition: Psoriasis is a chronic relapsing inflammatory skin condition. The most common form is characterized by scaly plaques, but there are important variations in how the disorder is manifested. Less common forms, such as generalized pustular psoriasis, may be life-threatening.

list.listitem: According to the National Psoriasis Foundation, between 150,000 and 260,000 new cases are diagnosed each year.
A systematic review reported an annual incidence rate of 41/100,000 person-year in children and 79/100,000 person-years in adults.
The National Psoriasis Foundation Benchmark Survey, completed in 2001 to 2002, showed a prevalence of 2.2% among adults in the United States.
A systematic review of global prevalence of psoriasis ranged from 0.5% to 11.4% in adults.
The same survey estimates that 4.5 million US adults have the disease, of which 1.5 million have moderate to severe disease.
The NIH estimates that as many as 7.5 million Americans are affected.
A systematic review found that the prevalence differed by country. In children, prevalence ranged from 0% to 2.1% (Italy) and in adults from 0.91% (United States) to 8.5% (Norway).
Psoriasis prevalence in African Americans was 1.3% compared to 2.5% of Caucasians.
Slightly more women than men are affected.
In 2013, the estimated annual cost of psoriasis in the U.S. ranged from $35 billion to $112 billion, with $11.2 billion in lost productivity.

According to the National Psoriasis Foundation Benchmark Survey, 77% of patients with moderate to severe psoriasis reported that the disease was a moderate to large problem in their lives, and one-third reported the disease was a very large problem.

In the same survey, 26% of respondents reported that the disease forced them to alter or stop normal daily activities, 40% reported that psoriasis affected their clothing choices, and 36% reported psoriasis affected their ability to sleep.
Psoriasis is an immunologically-mediated inflammatory condition.
Predisposition to psoriasis is thought to be genetically transmitted by autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance.
Psoriasis may arise spontaneously or be triggered by infection, drugs, or stress.
Chronic inflammation in the skin causes accelerated maturation of epidermal cells.
Chronic systemic inflammation and immunologic changes may be responsible for comorbidities.
Control cardiovascular risk factors, because patients with psoriasis have a higher risk of cardiovascular disease including myocardial infarction and other vascular diseases. C

A retrospective cohort study found that herpes zoster vaccine is safe in patients taking biologics and anti-TNF therapies. A systematic review of 42 studies concluded that recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) should be administered to all patients over the age of 50 with psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis, regardless of concurrent systemic or biologic therapy.B
Diagnosis is based on recognition of typical skin, nail, and scalp lesions (). C
Multiple forms of psoriasis exist, making it is essential to be familiar with the patterns of less common types including inverse psoriasis and palmoplantar psoriasis. C
Biopsy (typically a 3- to 4-mm punch) may be helpful to confirm diagnosis if the clinical picture is uncertain. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Less scaly than psoriasis without Auspitz's Sign
Small oval plaques in "Christmas-tree" distribution, "collarette scale"
Plaques more angular, purplish in color with reticular pattern of white lines
Atrophic epidermis in plaques with predilection for genital and perianal regions
Red papules coalescing to form large red plaques

list.listitem: The National Psoriasis Foundation (NPF) created the following classification based on percentage of body surface affected: mild <3%, moderate if 3% to 10%, and severe >10% or if it affects the palms or soles.
By the NPF criteria, 65% of patients have mild disease, 25% have moderate disease, and 8% have severe disease.
Diagnosis is made by recognizing the typical skin, nail, and scalp lesions.

The most commonly affected areas are the scalp, elbows, and legs (about 80% each), followed by the knees, arms, and trunk (50%-60% each). The palms and soles are affected in approximately 10% of patients.
The severity of disease is determined by the proportion of body surface area affected, along with specific location of lesions and impact on quality of life.

The Patient Report of Extent of Psoriasis Involvement (PREPI), a single-question method for measuring body surface area affected by psoriasis, has been shown to be reliable with high patient and physician agreement (ICC = 0.82) and responsiveness to change.

A 15-item patient questionnaire, the Psoriatic Arthritis Screening and Evaluation (PASE), had modest sensitivity (76%) and specificity (76%) using a score of 44 for differentiating patients with psoriatic arthritis from those with psoriasis alone. The authors postulate that this might be a good screening tool for early detection of psoriatic arthritis.

For psoriasis patients without known psoriatic arthritis (PsA), evidence shows that common screening questionnaires (PEST, CONTEST, and CONTESTjt) have similar moderate sensitivity (~54–63%) and specificity (~75–83%) for detecting undiagnosed PsA. No single tool is clearly superior, so clinicians should use a simple validated screener (eg, the 5-question PEST) to aid early PsA detection.
See for clinical features of different forms of psoriasis.
Biopsy may be useful but is only necessary when the clinical diagnosis is unclear.
A 3- to 4-mm punch biopsy of affected skin is preferred.
Diagnosis is made clinically () sometimes supplemented by 3- to 4-mm punch biopsy of affected area.
See for a recommended treatment strategy and for drug therapy.
Topical corticosteroid monotherapy or combination therapy with topical vitamin D/corticosteroid is the first line treatment for mild psoriasis. A
Consider phototherapy for extensive disease. B
Systemic therapies, including methotrexate and biologics, may be useful for extensive or resistant disease, but require close monitoring due to the potentially serious side effects. A
Biologic agents (monoclonal antibodies) are increasingly becoming the standard of care, particularly when other agents such as methotrexate have failed. A
Consider avoiding the use of systemic corticosteroids to treat psoriasis, but evidence is scant and not suggestive of its association with severe psoriasis flares. C
See for a suggested treatment algorithm and for drug therapy dosing.

Topical therapy is reasonable first-line treatment if the disease involves less than 20% of the body surface area. High-potency topical corticosteroids (Class 1 or 2) are the most commonly prescribed treatment. The vehicle should be adjusted to the skin type and the location of the lesions (overall NNT vs vehicle = 2).

To minimize systemic absorption, the amount applied should be limited to 50 grams per week, and the duration of therapy should be restricted to the shortest duration that provides significant relief. Steroid monotherapy is appropriate for disease that involves less than 10% of the body surface area.

A Cochrane Review in 2013 found corticosteroid monotherapy to be as effective as monotherapy with vitamin D analogues for the topical treatment of chronic plaque psoriasis, but with less local side effects (eg, burning, irritation). For both body and scalp psoriasis, combined vitamin D/corticosteroid therapy appears more effective than corticosteroid monotherapy or vitamin D monotherapy. Combination therapy and corticosteroid monotherapy have less local side effects compared to vitamin D monotherapy. For isolated scalp psoriasis, combination therapy and corticosteroid monotherapy are more effective and cause less side effects than vitamin D monotherapy. There is insufficient data on cutaneous dermal atrophy and long-term safety of corticosteroids for maintenance therapy. Vitamin D analogues do not appear to cause skin atrophy.

A network meta-analysis compared different topical therapies for plaque psoriasis of the body and scalp. The most effective therapies are potent corticosteroids (alone or combined with a vitamin D analogue) and very potent corticosteroids. Once daily application appears as effective as twice daily use. Continuous corticosteroid use for up to 8 weeks or intermittent use for a year appears safe, but longer-term safety data is lacking.
In the U.S., calcipotriene is the only FDA-approved synthetic vitamin D analogue for plaque psoriasis. It is available as monotherapy or in combination with corticosteroids.
Limited use of fluticasone propionate ointment, 0.005%, is effective and safe for use on the face and intertriginous areas of patients with small psoriatic plaques (<2 x 2 cm) up to 10 weeks.
For intertriginous psoriasis, betamethasone appears more effective than calcipotriene; calcipotriene is better than placebo; and pimecrolimus is minimally, if at all, effective.

Topical calcineurin inhibitors, tacrolimus and pimecrolimus, have been shown to be effective in small studies (tacrolimus 46% vs placebo 17%, NNT = 3.4). They may be useful in areas such as the face, where long-term use of topical steroids may not be desirable. Other studies found tacrolimus ointment 0.1% and pimecrolimus cream 1% to be effective in the treatment of facial and intertriginous psoriasis.
Tazarotene, a topical retinoid, is as effective as Class 2 topical steroids and more effective than placebo (42% vs placebo 24%, NNT = 5.5).

Tapinarof 1% cream (Vtama) is a topical interleukin-17 inhibitor. In a trial that randomized 1025 patients with mild to severe plaque psoriasis to tapinarof or vehicle, patients in the active therapy group were significantly more likely to report being clear or nearly clear at 12 weeks (35.4% vs 6.0% in trial 1, and 40.2% vs 6.2% in trial 2, p < 0.001, NNT = 3 for both trials). Adverse events were common including folliculitis (23%), contact dermatitis (5.0%), and headache (3.8%). Adverse events severe enough to withdraw from the study occurred in 5.7% in active treatment compared with 0.3% with vehicle. Tapinarof was approved in 2022 for adults with plaque psoriasis after phase III trials (PSOARING 1 and 2) showed significant efficacy.
Anthralin (or dithranol), present in goa powder derived from the araroba tree, is more effective than placebo for treating chronic plaque psoriasis, based on a Cochrane Review from 2013.
Coal tar is often used, but its effectiveness has not been proven.
Emollients and/or salicylic acid should be considered as adjunct therapies with any other treatments and may be used alone for mild disease.

Systemic therapy should be used for extensive disease or for localized disease resistant to treatment with topical agents and phototherapy. All systemic therapies have significant toxicities that must be considered when planning treatment. Methotrexate has been used extensively and is widely considered to be effective. Most studies are older and not methodologically sound.

Palmoplantar pustular psoriasis: A Cochrane Review in 2020 found insufficient evidence for the efficacy and safety of systemic therapy using acitretin, methotrexate and cyclosporine, and ultrapotent corticosteroids and phototherapy for treating chronic palmoplantar pustular psoriasis. Low-quality evidence suggests that maxacalcitol is better than placebo to achieve short-term clearance, while moderate-quality evidence demonstrates that oral alitretinoin is comparable to placebo in decreasing severity. As far as biological therapy for chronic palmoplantar pustular psoriasis, there is insufficient evidence on the efficacy of etanercept and ustekinumab, based on low-quality evidence. Secukinumab and guselkumab are likely more effective than placebo to reduce severity, based on moderate-quality evidence.

Generalized pustular psoriasis: A consensus guidelines recommends methotrexate, infliximab, acitretin, and cyclosporine as first-line treatments for generalized pustular psoriasis; adalimumab, etanercept and psoralen with UVA are recommended as alternatives. Spesolimab is under investigation, and in a randomized trial with 52 patients receiving a single 900 mg IV dose or placebo in a 2:1 ratio, the likelihood of Generalized Pustular Psoriasis Physician Global Assessment score of 0 or 1 at 1 week was higher in the treatment group (43% vs 11%, p = 0.02, NNT = 3).

Nail psoriasis: A Cochrane Review in 2013, based on low-certainty evidence, reported that infliximab, golimumab, and radiotherapy (using electron beam, grenz ray, and superficial radiotherapy) are likely better than comparative treatment for treating nail psoriasis. However, radiotherapy is not routinely used in clinical practice to treat nail psoriasis. And while the evidence for topical therapies is insufficient, it does not necessarily mean they are ineffective. A randomized trial with 198 patients with nail psoriasis compared 2 doses of secukinumab with placebo and found that secukinumab was superior at 16 weeks.

listitem.em: Methotrexate, oral fumaric acid esters, and acitretin

list.listitem: A Cochrane Review in 2019 found low-dose oral methotrexate (≤15 mg) to be slightly more effective than placebo for the short-term treatment (ie, 6 months) of psoriatic arthritis, based on low-quality evidence. Long-term efficacy and safety are uncertain, along with methotrexate's effects on important patient-oriented outcomes.

Cyclosporine is effective in both short-term induction and long-term maintenance therapy of psoriasis. Maintenance therapy should be used only where other options have proven ineffective. Cyclosporine has not been approved by the FDA for treatment of psoriasis.

A Cochrane Review in 2015 concluded that oral fumaric acid esters (FAEs) are superior to placebo and comparable to methotrexate for the treatment of psoriasis. No serious short-term side effects were noted; minor adverse events include flushing and gastrointestinal symptoms.

An RCT randomized adolescents age 10 to 17 years with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis to oral fumaric acid ester or placebo. At 20 weeks the clinical response rates were treater for active treatment (55% vs 19%, p < 0.001, NNT = 4). Adverse events were more common with fumaric acid ester, largely gastrointestinal.

Acitretin, a systemic retinoid, is effective, either as monotherapy or in combination with other agents (NNT vs placebo = 2). It is reported to be more effective for generalized pustular psoriasis or erythrodermic psoriasis than for plaque psoriasis.

listitem.em: Biologic therapies (Tumor necrosis factor and Interleukin inhibitors)

list.listitem: Biologic agents should be considered for moderate to severe psoriasis inadequately controlled by topical therapies and phototherapy, patients who have failed, have poor tolerance or contraindications to methotrexate and cyclosporine, patients whose lives are significantly affected by the disease (eg, Dermatology Life Quality Index [DLQI] >10, significant depression or anxiety), extensive disease (eg, body surface area (BSA) >10% or Psoriasis Area and Severity Index [PASI] ≥10), severe local disease with functional impairment and/or significant distress, patients with active psoriatic arthritis, and for persistent psoriasis.

British Academy of Dermatology guidelines (2020) recommend that biologics be administered by specialists in dermatology and the response to therapy be reviewed at least every 6 months. Therapy should be tailored using any licensed drug based on goals of therapy, patient factors, and drug costs. A decision aid is provided as a supplement to the guideline.

A network meta-analysis in support of the BAD 2020 guidelines reviewed biologic agents for their ability to achieve ≥90% reduction in PASI score in patients with moderate to severe psoriasis. They concluded that there was high short-term efficacy and tolerability for adalimumab, brodalumab, certolizumab pegoll, guselkumab, risankizumab, secukinumab, tildrakizumab, and ustekinumab. They concluded that infliximab and ixekizumab were also highly effective short-term, but were less well tolerated. Data regarding long-term efficacy and safety is lacking, and studies may not be representative of patients in typical practice given the young mean age of study participants (45 years) and high disease severity (PASI 20 at baseline).

Cochrane's network meta-analysis, based on high-certainty evidence, found infliximab, bimekizumab, ixekizumab, and risankizumab to be the most effective biologic agents for induction therapy (8 to 24 weeks) for moderate to severe chronic plaque psoriasis, compared to placebo. Severe adverse events were similar between these biologic agents and placebo, based on very low to moderate certainty evidence.

In a network meta-analysis of 52 short-term (12-16 week) and 7 long-term (48-56 week) RCTs of treatments for psoriasis. For short-term studies, serious adverse events were lowest for certrolizumab (0.8%), resankizumab (1.2%) and etanercept (1.6%). In short-term studies, risankizumab (0.5%), tildrakizumab (1.0%) and guselkumab (1.5%) were least likely to lead to treatment discontinuation. In long-term studies, risankizumab had the lowest rates of adverse events and treatment discontinuation.

A network meta-analysis of comparisons between biologics and oral treatments for moderate to severe plaque psoriasis concluded that brodalumab, guselkumab, ixekizumab and risankizumab were most likely to achieve a high PASI response.

A study randomized 743 patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis to bimekizumab 320 mg once monthly or secukinumab 300 mg weekly for one month and then monthly, both given subcutaneously.Patients given bimekizumab were more likely at 48 weeks to have 100% clearance (67% vs 46%, p < 0.001, NNT = 5). However, the risk of oral candidiasis was much higher with bimekizumab (19% vs 3%, NNH = 6). In the BE COMPLETE trial, 69% of patients (N=176) receiving bimekizumab therapy achieved 90% or greater improvement in PASI 90 scores compared to 7% of patients receiving placebo (adusted odds ratio 30, 95% CI 12.4-74).

Biologic agents include efalizumab (efficacy 27% vs placebo 4%, NNT = 4.3 in one study and absolute risk difference 24% (19%-30%) in a systematic review),etanercept (at 24 weeks 56% vs placebo 5%, NNT = 2 in one study and absolute risk difference 30% (25%-35%) in a systematic review), infliximab (88% vs placebo 7%, NNT = 1.2 in one study and absolute risk difference 77% (72%-81%) in a systematic review), and adalimumab (71% vs placebo 7%, NNT = 1.6 in one study and absolute risk difference 64% (61%-68%) in a systematic review).
In patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, adding methotrexate to etanercept improved the likelihood of clearance at 12 weeks somewhat (NNT = 5), but with more adverse events (NNH = 6).

Icotrokinra binds IL-23. A trial randomized 684 persons 12 and older with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis to icotrokinra or placebo in a 2:1 ratio. At week 16 a 90% improvement in Psoriasis Area Severity Index was seen more often with active drug (50% vs 4%, p < 0.001, NNT = 2). Adverse events were generally mild and similar between groups.

Adalimumab was evaluated for safety and efficacy in moderate to severe fingernail psoriasis and plaque psoriasis. Patients were randomized to 40mg adalimumab every other week or placebo. Primary endpoint was 75% improvement in nail psoriasis severity index (NAPSI score). Of 217 patients, 188 (87%) completed 26 weeks of treatment or moved to open labelled period. 47% of adalimumab patients compared to 3.4% of placebo met primary end point (p <0.001). Nail pain, functioning severity and global assessment also improved. Serious infection rates were 1.9% placebo vs 3.7% adalimumab group. At 52 weeks, serious adverse events and serious infection rates for the adalimumab group (n = 203) were 6.9% and 3.4% respectively.

Secukinumab showed superior efficacy compared to ustekinumab in 676 randomized double blinded patients at week 52 with PASI-90 76% vs 61% (p <0.0001) and PASI-100 46% vs 36% (p = 0.103). At week 52, 72% of patients on secukinumab vs 59% on ustekinumab (p = 0.008) reported no impact of skin disease on their lives. A meta-analysis found secukinumab 150mg and 300mg both equally tolerable without significant adverse drug events reported with either dosage. Secukinumab was also superior to fumaric acid esters in a 24 week single-blinded RCT with 200 patients, with higher response rates (89% vs 34%, p <0.001, NNT = 2) and fewer adverse events (2% vs 33%).

Guselkumab, an anti-IL-23 human monoclonal antibody, was compared with adalimumab for moderate to severe plaque psoriasis showing significant improvement in scalp and palmoplantar psoriasis. Patients were randomized to guselkumab 100mg (weeks 0, 4 and then every 8 weeks) or placebo followed by guselkumab 100mg starting at week 16 or adalimumab (80mg week 0 and 40 mg week 1 and then every 2 weeks) and then assessed for 24 weeks. Of 1829 patients, guselkumab was superior to placebo at week 16 for scalp psoriasis and to adalimumab at week 24 (both p <0.001). 153 (75%) patients in the guselkumab group vs 76 (50%) with adalimumab at week 24 had hand and foot psoriasis scores of 0 (p <0.001). Fingernail psoriasis showed no statistical difference.
Guselkumab was also superior to placebo for pediatric patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis in a trial with 92 patients. PASI 90 was 56% vs 16% at 16 weeks. Safety profile was good.

A double-blinded RCT of 1,048 patients compared rates of reported PASI-90 at week 48 between randomized patients with moderate-to-severe plaque-type psoriasis receiving either guselkumab or secukinumab at the recommended doses. Findings showed greater response in the guselkumab group (N = 451 [84%]) compared to the secukinumab group (N = 360 [70%]; p <0.0001).

Risankizumab, an anti-IL-23 human monoclonal antibody, was compared to adalimumab in a double-blinded RCT of 605 patients with primary endpoint being a reduction of at least 90% in the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI-90) at 16 weeks of therapy. Results showed that 72% of patients taking risankizumab achieved PASI-90 compared to 47% of those taking adalimumab (95% CI, 17.5-32.4; p <0.0001).

An open label randomized trial of 352 patients with moderate plaque psoriasis sponsored by the manufacturer of risankizumab found that investigator assessed PASI-90 occurred more often with risankizumab than with apremilast 30 mg twice daily (56% vs 5%).

Patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis were randomized (n=255) to placebo or one of 5 doses of JNJ-77242113, an oral IL-23 antagonist peptide. Response rates using PASI 75 as the outcome were higher for the active treatment groups (range 37% to 79% vs 9%).

Certolizumab is an anti TNF monoclonal antibody. In a pooled analysis of 3 RCTs with 144 weeks of follow-up for patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, both 200 mg and 400 mg doses had good efficacy (71% - 73% vs 43% - 49% treatment success, NNT = 3 to 4). There were also no major safety concerns.
Alefacept (Amevive) is a weekly injectable agent that may slightly improve symptoms for patients with chronic plaque psoriasis.

It is important to test patients for tuberculosis before using a biologic agent. In one retrospective study of 50 patients (90% had been given BCG) requiring tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor treatment for psoriasis, 20% tested positive for latent TB; the interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) (T-Spot.TB) was a more accurate test than the TB skin test for detection.

listitem.em: Janus-associated kinase (JAK) and tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs)

list.listitem: Tofacitinib is an oral Janus-associated kinase (JAK) inhibitor, and has shown to be effective in improving health-related quality of life in 2 one-year RCTs (NNT ~3). An RCT randomized 422 patients with an inadequate response to conventional DMARDs to tofacitinib, adalimumab, or placebo. Both active drugs were more effective than placebo, but there was no difference with regards to efficacy between tofacitinib and adalimumab.

Deucravacitinib is an oral tyrosine kinase 2 inhibitor. A trial randomized 1020 patients with moderate to severe plaque psoriasis to deucravacitinib 6 mg daily, apremilast 30 mg twice daily, or placeo. After 16 weeks, a reduction of at least 75% in the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI-75) was achieved in 53% in the deucravacitinib group, 39.8% in the apremilast group, and 9.4% in the placebo group.

Apremilast, an oral phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitor, significantly reduces severity of moderate to severe adult psoriasis for up to 52 weeks. 75% PASI score reduction from baseline was seen in 33% on apremilast (10 mg daily titrated up to 30 mg BD) vs 5% in placebo (NNT = 3.6; 95% CI, 3.1-4.4). Discontinuation due to adverse events (8%) were similar in both placebo and apremilast groups. Apremilast can reduce the severity of scalp and nail psoriasis at 16 weeks versus placebo.

Apremilast demonstrated acceptable safety profile and well tolerated for >156 weeks in a randomized controlled study. Adverse events in 5% patients within 52 weeks included nausea, diarrhea, headaches and upper respiratory infections. No new AE were reported by 156 weeks.

In a RCT of 303 adults with moderate to severe scalp psoriasis intolerant of at least one other drug were randomized to oral apremilast or placebo. There significant responses in the global assessment (43% vs 14%, NNT = 3) as well as on scalp and whole body itch scores (NNT = 4-5).

In a randomized double-blinded controlled trial, roflumiast 0.3% topical cream demonstrated scores on the validated Investigator's Global Assessment (IGA) consistent with clear or almost clear disease 6 weeks in 28% of the patients compared to 8% in placebo (NNT = 5, P <0.001).

A pair of RCTs randomized 439 and 442 patients with plaque psoriasis covering 2% to 20% of their body to roflumilast cream 0.3% or vehicle. Success was defined as at least 2 grades on a 4 point investigator assessed scale. This occurred significantly more often in both trials: trial 1 42.4% vs 6.1%, trial 2 37.5% vs 6.9%. Adverse events were similar to vehicle.
A roflumilast 0.3% foam was effective in an RCT with 304 participants with scalp and body psoriasis, with a response of 59% vs 11% for vehicle at 8 weeks.

A small RCT randomized 21 persons with intertriginous, anogenital, or facial psoriasis to the topic PDE4 inhibitor crisaborole 2% or vehicle cream, and found greater improvement at one month with active treatment. Larger trials are needed.

While Streptococcal infection may precipitate guttate psoriasis and exacerbate chronic plaque psoriasis, there is no firm evidence to support the use of antibiotics or tonsillectomy as effective and safe interventions for guttate and chronic plaque psoriasis. No RCTs directly evaluated the efficacy and safety of amoxicillin and penicillin V for psoriasis. Furthermore, there is lack of evidence for the use of topical and systemic medications, biotherapy or phototherapy in the treatment of acute guttate psoriasis or the management of acute guttate flare of chronic psoriasis.

A systematic review examined the evidence regarding plant extracts in the treatment of psoriasis concluded that there is limited evidence to support the use of M. aquifolium, indigo naturalis and Aloe vera, but serious adverse events were not reported.

A Cochrane Review in 2019 found low-quality evidence that dietary intervention may decrease psoriasis severity and moderate-quality evidence that dietary intervention may improve quality of life and reduce BMI in obese psoriatic patients compared to usual care. Combined dietary intervention and exercise program may decrease psoriasis severity and BMI compared to providing information only. Adherence appears better with the dietary intervention group compared to usual care, while adherence to combined diet and exercise appears similar to those who were only provided information.

The three common phototherapy types used to treat extensive psoriasis include narrow-band ultraviolet B (NB-UVB), broad-band ultraviolet B (BB-UVB), and psoralen ultraviolet A photochemotherapy (PUVA). Prior to phototherapy, psoralen is a photosensitizer that can be administered orally or applied topically or as a bath.

A Cochrane Review in 2013 found significant heterogeneity and inconsistent evidence when comparing oral PUVA and NB-UVB, and when comparing bath PUVA and NB-UVB. PUVA plus retinoid is as effective as NB-UVB plus retinoid for chronic plaque psoriasis and guttate psoriasis. NB-UVB and selective BB-UVB appear similarly effective in clearing chronic plaque psoriasis.

A Cochrane Review in 2020, based on low-certainty evidence, concluded that indoor salt bath followed by artificial UVB phototherapy (mimicking sea bathing followed by sun bathing) may be more effective than UVB phototherapy alone for treating chronic plaque psoriasis; both have similar side effects.
Topical therapies should be used as needed to control lesions.
Systemic treatments should be used to induce remission, and then reduced to the lowest effective dose for maintenance.
Refer patients with localized disease not responding to topical therapy to a dermatologist, as well as patients with extensive disease requiring phototherapy or systemic therapy.

The primary complication of psoriasis is a significant decrease in the quality of life for the affected patient. The effect on quality of life has been found to be as great as for other severe illnesses, such as some cancers, coronary artery disease, and chronic pulmonary disease. Attention to depression and stress is important in helping patients manage this illness.

Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a common comorbidity of psoriasis that can substantially affect quality of life. Updated estimates indicate that approximately 20–30% of psoriasis patients (up to one-third) will develop PsA over time. A Cochrane review found TNF inhibitors very effective for PsA, leading to significant clinical improvement, diminished disease activity, modest improvement in radiographic progression, and improvement in quality of life compared to placebo (moderate-certainty evidence).

In terms of metabolic comorbidities, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) has emerged as a significant comorbidity of psoriasis. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 41 studies (over 600,000 individuals) found a pooled NAFLD prevalence of ~29.5% among adult psoriasis patients, and about 1.7-fold higher odds of NAFLD compared to people without psoriasis. ​

Psoriasis imposes a substantial psychosocial burden, with higher rates of depression and anxiety observed in affected patients. Importantly, improvement in skin disease can translate into mental health benefits. A recent prospective study assessed depression and anxiety in psoriasis patients starting biologic therapy. At baseline, patients had significantly more symptoms of depression and anxiety than non-psoriatic controls, and greater skin severity correlated with worse mood scores. After 6 months of biologic treatment, there was a significant reduction in disease severity (PASI and DLQI) and a parallel improvement in mental health – depression and anxiety scores dropped markedly (p < 0.0001) from pre-treatment levels. In fact, improvements in PASI were significantly associated with lower depression/anxiety scores, highlighting that effective treatment can alleviate psychological comorbidities. No particular biologic agent was superior in this regard​.

Avoid using systemic corticosteroids to treat psoriasis, but evidence is scant and not suggestive of its association with severe psoriasis flares. Use of systemic steroids for extensive psoriasis or during acute exacerbation may cause a pustular or erythrodermic flare, which can be severe and potentially life-threatening. Psoriasis may also worsen due to withdrawal of systemic steroid therapy, known as rebound flare. While it is common knowledge among dermatologists not to use systemic steroids for psoriasis, there is paucity of evidence for this. In general, use ultrapotent topical steroids to control an outbreak. Acitretin generally produces the most rapid relief from pustular psoriasis, but methotrexate or cyclosporine are other options to consider.

Patients with severe erythrodermic or pustular psoriasis often require inpatient management with intravenous fluids to prevent dehydration. The health care team should also be alert for signs of septicemia.
Oral acitretin provides the most rapid response for both conditions; IV methotrexate and cyclosporine are alternative treatments.
Plaque psoriasis is normally a chronic, indolent disease with intermittent waxing and waning. C
Decrease in quality of life may be a significant factor in this illness. C
Relapses are common when any therapy is stopped. C
Pustular and erythrodermic psoriasis can be life-threatening and should be managed by a dermatologist with hospitalization or close outpatient follow-up. C
Plaque psoriasis is normally a chronic indolent disease, with intermittent waxing and waning.
Untreated generalized pustular psoriasis may be fatal.

Approximately 5% to 8% of people with skin disease develop psoriatic arthritis, which may be a serious erosive arthritis. In one cohort study, features associated with a higher likelihood of psoriatic arthritis were scalp lesions (hazard ratio [HR] = 3.89; 95% CI, 2.18-6.94), nail dystrophy (HR = 2.93; 95% CI, 1.68-5.12), and intergluteal/perianal psoriasis (HR = 2.35; 95% CI, 1.32-4.19).
Plaque psoriasis is generally considered to be a chronic and persistent disease.
Except in mild cases, the need for treatment will be lifelong.
Close follow-up and aggressive treatment of psoriasis may be important for effective management of the disease. No specific follow-up intervals are recommended.

According to the NPF Benchmark Survey, patients with psoriasis frequently change physicians, reflecting low satisfaction with treatment. About 3% of patients with the disease say they are very dissatisfied with their overall treatment, and half of these patients have moderate to severe disease. Only 35% of people with moderate to severe disease have ever tried phototherapy or common systemic therapies, and only 22% are currently using these modalities.

There is an increased risk of diabetes (RR = 1.63; 95% CI, 1.25-2.12) and hypertension (1.17; 95% CI, 1.06-1.30) among women with psoriasis. Additionally, a meta-analysis of 16 studies demonstrated a statistically significant correlation between hypertension risk and diagnosis of psoriasis (OR 1.43; 95% CI, 1.25–1.64).

Like those with any chronic illness, patients with psoriasis benefit from a close working relationship with their healthcare provider. The statistics suggest that many patients are not being treated in an appropriately aggressive manner, but there are no data to show the sources of the deficiencies in care.
The physician should help the patient set realistic personal goals for control of the illness, as well as strategies for identifying exacerbations and changing therapy when they occur.

Since stress may trigger exacerbations, and since depression and anxiety are common disease comorbidities, patients should be encouraged to work on stress management, to be attentive to symptoms of psychological illness, and to discuss these issues with their healthcare providers.
Support groups may be helpful for patients in learning to cope with the illness.

The web site of the National Psoriasis Foundation, www.psoriasis.org, has a large amount of information for patients, including educational materials, tools for finding support groups, and links to other resources.
Acitretin, tazarotene, and methotrexate are listed as Pregnancy Class X agents by the FDA.
All other drugs are Pregnancy Class B or C.

Guttate psoriasis is often preceded by streptococcal pharyngitis or a viral URI. While this disorder often resolves spontaneously, it may be the first sign that the patient is at risk for developing chronic psoriasis in the future.
Methotrexate is considered the systemic treatment of choice for childhood psoriasis.

One RCT found etanercept to be an effective treatment for plaque psoriasis in children poorly controlled on topical therapy; 75% improvement was seen in 57% of patients in the treatment group vs 11% of those in the control group.
A Cochrane Review in 2015 concluded, based on only one RCT, that etanercept appears to be effective and safe in the short-term treatment of pediatric psoriasis.

cell.label: Mild disease involving <20% of body surface area?
Start topical steroids alone or with one of following: calcipotriene or tazarotene. Effective?
Use topical steroid as pulse therapy on weekend and other agent during the week.
Start clobetasol ointment and refer for narrow-band UV therapy. Effective?
Refer for methotrexate, acitretin, biologic agent, or cyclosporine.
Taper clobetasol to weekends only and continue UV for 4 months.

feature.caption: Clinical Features of Different Forms of Psoriasis.

tr.td: 80%-90% of patients have this form of the disease
Red scaly papules coalesce to form oval plaques
Plaques are covered in white scale. Removal of scale reveals bleeding point (Auspitz' sign)
Plaques may be localized or diffuse
Extensor surfaces are affected more than flexor surfaces
Palms and soles are usually spared
Course is generally chronic and stable
May be the only site affected
Appearance similar to plaque psoriasis, but scales may be anchored to hairs and harder to remove
Abrupt onset, often following a viral upper respiratory infection or streptococcal pharyngitis
Lesions are erythematous scaly papules, pinpoint to 1 cm in size
Face and scalp may be involved
May resolve in weeks to months
Disease may affect flexural or intertriginous areas
Axillae, groin, under breasts, behind ears
Red, smooth plaques confined to skin folds
May be induced by infection or friction as a form of Koebner's phenomenon
May be confused with candidal infection
May be an isolated finding or part of more generalized involvement
Plaques are red with thick brown scale
May be confused with chronic eczema
Usually occurs in patients with pre-existing disease
May be triggered by stopping systemic steroids or other systemic therapies, overuse of topical steroids or other irritating topical medications, phototherapy, or infection
May affect palms and soles or be localized to digits
Lesions start on palms and soles or in flexion creases, then become generalized
Starts as small sterile pustules on an erythematous base that coalesce to form larger collections of pus
Patient is toxic and febrile with an elevated WBC count
Stopping topical or oral steroids may precipitate a flare
Pitting is the most common finding
Fragmentation and crumbling of nails or separation of the nail from the bed may be seen
“Oil-spot lesion” is a yellowish discoloration caused by localized separation of the nail from the nail bed, with trapping of sebum and cellular debris
More extensive subungual debris may accumulate, separating the distal nail from the nail bed
Initial: 50 mg twice weekly for 3 months sc
Initial: 5 mg/kg IV at 0, 2, and 6 weeks
